We named the X515 our low-wattage value pick in our Best Chargers article, beating several comparables. Overall, it’s a solid choice for anyone who needs a high-quality multi-port USB wall charger. And being well over 40% off makes this a steal for its class. – Joe Shields

SanDisk’s WD Black SN8100 clone, the 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 SSD, is on sale for almost $95 off its typical price and at an all-time low, according to Amazon. For $349, you can get one of the faster 2TB drives. At less than $ 0.18 per GB, it’s one of the cheapest 2TB PCIe 5.0 drives available right now. The drive reaches speeds up to 14,900/14,000 MB/s (read/writes), nearly saturating PCIe 5.0 bandwidth.

Expand your internal storage with Sandisk's 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD. This speedy drive offers 14,900/14,000 r/w speeds and has a 5-year warranty.

Whether you use it as your primary OS drive or to store your most frequently accessed games, the SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB is an excellent option for a new PC or even upgrading your current storage. At an all-time low price of $349.99 (less than $0.18 per GB), it’s not only fast (faster than the Samsung 9100 Pro), but the price is right, too. – Joe Shields

It's all about speed. If you're streaming at 4K, or playing games online where latency can kill you before your opponents can, then you need fast networking. This TP-Link 5-port switch, down to just $7.99, can unlock an extra four gigabit Ethernet ports to your network for your PC, laptop, game consoles, and more.

All you need to do to use this unmanaged switch is to switch it on and hook it up to your router using one of the ports. If you're stuck with slow Wi-Fi, especially in a congested area, there isn't a better alternative. You'll be able to max out your internet connection's bandwidth with a faster wired network this way.

The TP-Link Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch LS1005G provides four additional Ethernet ports, delivering reliable, high-speed wired internet for your gaming PC, NAS, console, TV, and other connected devices. Another popular Tom's Hardware recommendation and one that several of us own ourselves.

This is a plug-and-play option that doesn't need configuring, so it's perfect for a beginner and a pro. If you're struggling with lag or slow connectivity on your local network, then this $8 switch (along with some Ethernet cables) is an easy solution, and at a great price. — Ben Stockton

HP's HyperX gaming brand is known for its good quality peripherals, including gaming mics, which are easy to use and usually sound great. Right now, the HyperX SoloCast 2 is on sale, and it's down to just $44.98.

This USB condenser mic has just one polar pattern (cardioid); it's designed to pick up just one person's voice in front of it. It's well built, made of a solid black cylinder with a metal grille, weighing almost 13 ounces (365.7g). Unlike most mics, this has a built-in stand, which you can tilt back by around 40 degrees to angle it right at your face. It's backed with rubber at the bottom, too, so it won't slip around, with mounting points if you want to add it to a boom arm.

This 14mm electret condenser capsule mic features an integrated desktop stand that tilts the mic upward 40 degrees (there's a mounting point on the bottom of the stand, in case you do want to mount it on a boom arm). It has a cardioid polar pattern and sounds pretty good out of the box, and it features HyperX's signature tap-to-mute button on the top.

There's a USB-C port on the back, with a large tap-to-mute button on top for easy access, along with a red indicator light to let you know when you're muted. It records at a high-res 24-bit, 96 kHz bit-depth and sample rate, sounding very good out of the box. There's also a built-in internal shock mount and pop filter, although it's better mounted rather than sitting on your desk.

This HyperX mic is simple and a good starter option for a gamer or office worker, and thanks to the $44.98 sale price, it's cheaper than ever. You can check out our HyperX SoloCast 2 review to learn more. — Ben Stockton

Want to try out VR? Then Meta's budget-friendly Meta Quest 3S should enter your checkout. Thanks to Black Friday, it's on sale for just $297.49 right now at Newegg, a 15% price drop compared to its usual price. You're also scoring a $15 gift card that you can use to put towards another Newegg purchase.

The Meta Quest 3S is the most affordable VR headset from Meta. Despite that, it still comes with the same CPU, RAM, and base storage as the most expensive Meta Quest 3, while also offering a slightly better battery life.

The Meta Quest 3S is a completely wireless experience, so there aren't any cables or cords to worry about here, and you don't need a PC to power it. It's got a smaller battery compared to the Meta Quest 3, but this VR headset should still last for 2.5 hours with continuous use.

The controllers, meanwhile, are powered by a single alkaline AA battery each. It's probably worth keeping a few extra rechargeable lithium-ion batteries close at hand, though, so you don't get cut off mid-way through a game. The Meta Quest 3S would make for a great gift this holiday season, for yourself or for a loved one, especially with that 15% discount on top. — Ben Stockton

Another Black Friday deal is here for those audiophiles needing an upgrade to their desk audio setup. These Edifier M60 PC speakers are back down to $149.99 on Amazon right now. That's a $50 off the retail price and it brings it back down to record lows, a price we last saw during Amazon's October sale.

The Edifier M60 speakers come with 3-inch mid-low drivers and 1-inch tweeters, and they're relatively compact, measuring just 6.6 inches (168mm) high by 3.9 inches (100mm) wide. They come with a pair of aluminum speaker stands that angle the speakers up by 15 degrees, pointing them directly toward your ears when they're placed at a desk.

This pair of compact desktop stereo speakers features USB-C, AUX, and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity, as well as touch controls and a built-in DSP. And they're on sale for their lowest price ever.

You can connect in a few different ways with the M60s, including by USB-C or traditional aux inputs, as well as by using Bluetooth 5.3. If you use Bluetooth, you can stream high-res audio (24-bit / 96 kHz) from mobile devices running Android 8 or later, too.

The speakers have a built-in DSP and touch controls that'll light up when you move your hand over them. With a total output power of 66W RMS, these aren't the most powerful PC speakers in the world, but they'll be a massive step up over listening through your laptop (or, worse, monitor's) tinny speakers. — Ben Stockton

There haven't been a huge amount of GPU deals during this Black Friday sales event, so this is a rare one. For $619, you can pick up this PowerColor RX 9070 GRE. It's the cheapest you'll find this GPU and, more importantly, it's a solid mid-tier performer for gaming at 1080p and 1440p at a far better price than rival GPUs like the RTX 5060 Ti.

This Radeon RX 9070 GRE is delivering great 1080p and 1440p gaming performance at a low price in today's market, giving you access to AMD's high-quality FSR 4 upscaler for a performance boost when you need it.

Our GPU hierarchy tests saw the RX 9070 GRE hit 90 FPS on average during all of our raster and ray tracing tests at 1080p, while also reaching 60 FPS at 1440p. Given the cost of this card, that's a really solid performance, especially as you might pay hundreds of dollars more for a rival Nvidia card to match it.

The 9070 GRE is an even better performer for pure raster gaming, hitting 120 FPS at 1080p and 90 FPS at 1440p, and that's before you even consider AMD's FSR 4 upscaling tech. If you want a quick, cheap and well-performing GPU upgrade for Black Friday, this PowerColor Reaper card might be one of the best ways to do it.

Dust: the enemy of all PCs. Dust is the perennial problem for PC owners, and once it builds up in your PC, it can cause it to overheat. Cleaning your rig regularly is the best course of action but, rather than rely on compressed air cans, you can invest in a compressed air duster, like this discounted Wolfbox MF50 for just $29.06, a new record low price for Black Friday.

An electric air duster, providing you with your own infinite supply of compressed air.

With this, you can banish the cans of compressed air and instead delete dust bunnies from your PC, along with any food or grime from your keyboard, along with any other areas of dirt collection on your desk. This portable and economical tool will keep your tech clean and tidy.

You can charge it over USB C in just 3.5 hours. It has a "turbo" fan that can reach speeds of up to 110,000 RPM, which provides up to four hours of use at its lowest setting. The MP50 has simple push controls, but all you really need to do is point and fire. There are four nozzles that'll help you control the airflow during a clean, too. — Ben Stockton

One of our favorite budget gaming chairs is now at an even better price for Black Friday. You can pick up the Razer Iskur V2 X for just $214.99 right now, a price drop of $85 compared to its usual list price.

The budget-friendly alternative to the Iskur V2, the Razer Iskur V2 X is a no-frills alternative that drives the price down by removing some of the adjustability options. That said, this chair still comes with built-in lumbar support, 2D armrests, and a 152-degree recline.

As our Razer Iskur V2 X review explains, this is the slightly less luxurious version of the OG Iskur V2. That does mean you have to accept a few compromises, but it's otherwise the same high-quality construction that we saw when we reviewed the original.

You're getting significant support on the base and back, high-density foam for the seat cushion, and adjustable 2D armrests here. Grab this steal of a Razer gaming chair at this price while you can. -- Ben Stockton

If you're traveling, you'll want a beefy portable power bank to fall back on to keep all of your devices charged. That's where this Ugreen Nexode 20,000 mAh power bank comes into play. It's on sale right now for $54.99, a new record low price that knocks $35 off the list price.

The UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank supports up to 130W of combined power output and features two USB-C and one USB-A port.

This power bank supports up to 100W of total power output across its two USB-C ports, but there's also a USB-A port for legacy devices that need charging. However, the different ports do have different max power levels: USB-C port 1 will give you 100W, while USB-C port 2 is capped at 65W, with the USB-A port at 22.5W max. According to Ugreen, this power bank can recharge a 13-inch MacBook Air up to 1.3 times if it's fully charged, or it can recharge an iPhone 16 Pro up to 3.7 times.

This Nexode bank also comes with a LCD display that'll tell you the current charge level of the battery, along with power output levels and the time remaining until the battery is discharged (or fully charged if it's charging). $54.99 for peace of mind while you're traveling isn't a bad option. — Ben Stockton

Power outages aren't fun, but they're especially not fun for your gaming PC. An outage can cause everything from lost data to electrical damage, but not if you buy this CyberPower UPS. It's on sale for $99.95 right now, a 29% price drop, bringing it down to a price we've not seen since 2023, according to Camelcamelcamel's price data.

This 900 V / 500 W battery backup protects up to six devices from a power outage, with a further six outlets offering surge protection. It has two USB charging ports.

This UPS battery pack is rated for 900 VA / 500 W and comes with 12 outlets. Six of them include both the battery backup protection, meaning you'll continue to have power after your electricity goes out, with an additional six offering just surge protection.

The pack also has spaced-out outlets for bigger plugs, along with two USB ports for charging. It has a three year warranty, along with a $125,000 guarantee to protect any devices you connect up to it. — Ben Stockton

Struggling with bad Wi-Fi? You need a router upgrade, and this TP-Link Archer BE550 for $149.99 is the answer, with a $100 saving to sink your teeth into. You're getting a ri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, able to provide up to 2,000 square feet of coverage, and fully expandable with EasyMesh-compatible devices.

You're able to get a combined maximum theoretical speed of 9.3 Gbps, split across the 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi 7, along with 5 and 2.4 GHz. If you're using a recent-enough device, Multi-Link Operation (or MLO) means you're able to use the different bands, like 5 GHz and 6 GHz, simultaneously for faster speeds and greater reliability.

The TP-Link Archer BE550 router packs six antennas, unlocking Wi-Fi 7 support for your network, with five 2.5 Gb Ethernet ports to help you future-proof your home network.

There are five 2.5 Gb Ethernet ports included in this BE550. One is the WAN port, so you'll use it to hook it up to your internet connection, along with four others that'll work for local devices like your gaming PC.

This router has everything you'd expect from a modern, mainstream Wi-Fi 7 router. It's got a USB port, too, that you can use for a quick-and-easy NAS solution using an external hard drive. Support for a mesh-style network, with per-device Quality of Service controls, mean you can set up priority for traffic for certain devices on a busy network, too. — Ben Stockton

Yes, AI has consumed the storage market, and hard drives have become pretty expensive these days, making it tough to be a humble data hoarder. While we've seen better storage deals in previous years, this $399.99 sale price for a 16TB Seagate Expansion external HDD is a good price in the current market.

The Seagate Expansion Desktop drive is a 16TB HDD that connects via USB 3.0. It's formatted to ExFAT by default, allowing it to work with virtually platform out of the box.

You can expect to pay hundreds of dollars more than this right now for a 16TB hard drive. Compare and contrast: for $399.99, this drive comes in at $0.02 per GB, which is a pretty sizable discount. Seagate doesn't disclose what model of drive it uses here, but these drives are typically shuckable.

That means that, if you want to break the 3.5-inch hard drive out of this enclosure, you can use it in your PC internally using SATA. This will void the warranty but it could be a good option if you need a lot of storage for your media files. — Ben Stockton

We've seen the price rises hit Apple's MacBook range, but Amazon has cut its prices back for Black Friday. A good option for buyers looking for an upgrade right now is the MacBook Air with the M5 chip. Earlier, we brought you the $999 512GB version; now the 1TB version is $400 off.

This is a go-to everyday laptop with premium build quality, a good trackpad, and solid battery life. It's a no-brainer for anyone looking for a step up from the MacBook Neo, with a bit more computing heft for everyday tasks, as long as you can handle the display's notch.

The M5 MacBook Air offers 1TB of storage, a 13-inch Retina display, and a 10-core CPU and 8-Core GPU with 16GB of unified memory that can take on pretty much all everyday tasks with ease.

This model scored highly in our MacBook Air M5 review earlier in the year, and its great value was one of the big reasons why. At under $1,200, that value prospect is even better. You've got frills like MagSafe charging, high-quality speakers and a comfortable keyboard and trackpad to work with, too. This is a laptop that'll suit most people, and for $1,199, it's $400 less than what it cost just a few months ago. — Ben Stockton

There's an ultra-light gaming mouse in your future, if you want it. Logitech's award-winning, ultra-light G Pro X Superlight 2 is on sale right now for just $69, down from $139.99. This near half-price saving unlocks a pseudo-ambidextrous wireless gaming mouse that weighs just 2.12 ounces (60g) and sports the company's Hero 2 optical sensor.

Logitech's ultralight 60g wireless mouse features a pseudo-ambidextrous symmetrical shape and sports the brand's Hero 2 optical sensor and Lightforce hybrid optical/mechanical switches.

The G Pro X Superlight 2 is ultra sensitive, up to 32,000 DPI, with a maximum speed of 500 IPS, and can handle up to 40 G's of force. It has a lightweight plastic shell with a smooth, soft-touch finish, and comes with five programmable buttons for macros or shortcuts.

The primary buttons use Logitech's Lightforce hybrid mechanical/optical switches, which are tactile and clicky (and a little loud). You can check out our Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 review if you're still unsure, but either way, $69 is a bargain for a no-nonsense mouse for competitive gaming. — Ben Stockton

If you've got a Mac Mini, or you're treating yourself to one over Black Friday, you can expand it pretty easily using a docking station. This Ugreen model is on sale for $49.99 right now, a 21% saving compared to its usual price.

This Ugreen dock has 11 different ports, as well as an SD card reader and room for an NVMe M.2 SSD.

This dock sits below the Mac Mini, connecting to its high-speed Thunderbolt port. It has several ports, including five USB-A 3.2 ports (rated for a mix of 10 and 5 Gbps), as well as two USB-C 3.2 (10 Gbps) and an SD card reader. It's also an enclosure for an additional M.2 NVMe SSD, giving your Mac Mini a quick and easy storage boost, although you'll need to supply your own drive.

This Ugreen dock supports recent-gen Mac Minis with M6, M5 Pro, and M4 chips. — Ben Stockton

Regularly priced at $449.99, Logitech’s Z906 5.1 surround sound system has had $50 knocked off the price, making the 1000W system now only $399.99. This is the lowest price in a while, but nothing near its all-time low of 2017. This model of speakers has been around for a long time now, but with few alternative 5.1 surround sound setups on the market, they still prove to be a popular choice.

Experience full surround sound on your PC when playing games or watching movies. This THX-certified system features a whopping 1000W of peak power output or 500W RMS. Five speakers, a subwoofer, a control box, and a remote control are all part of the package.

This 5.1 surround-sound set of speakers from Logitech contains 5 speakers plus a subwoofer and control box. Highlights of this setup include an impressive 1000W peak power and 500W RMS for room-filling sound, THX certification for the best soundstage, which is perfect for movie night, and a wireless remote control to easily changing volumes and channels when sat away from the PC and control box.

You can connect up to 6 devices at once and have individual control of each speaker via the control box to optimise sound. Make sure to position the five satellite speakers around your room for full immersion in whatever media you’re enjoying.

The closest PC surround sound speaker setup to this is the Arena 9 from SteelSeries, and although and very good set of speakers, the current price tag is $679.99 direct from SteelSeries, making the Logitech Z906 and very attractive proposition at just $399.99. — Stewart Bendle

While the Elgato Stream Deck MK.2 might, at first, appear to be a tool used for streamers and content creators, the customizable nature of the macropad makes it incredibly useful for anyone who sits and works at their desk every day. With configurable buttons and macros, including widespread community support, you can expect to configure heaps of plugins, assign hotkeys, and more across the 15-key keypad.

Built for streamers and content creators, the Elgato Stream Deck MK.2 is a purpose-built macro pad offering 15 LCD keys and widespread software support for a slew of additional plugins.

We reviewed the Stream Deck MK.2 when it was released in 2021, and called out how well it managed to streamline the process of streaming, thanks to the LCD keypad, USB-C connectivity, revised angle, and customizable plates. For anyone doing serious work at a desk, this is an ideal gift to add to their setup, even if they don't do any streaming or content creation. — Sayem Ahmed

The GameSir Cyclone 2 is a wireless controller with TMR joysticks and micro-trigger buttons, and you can save 20% off it for Cyber Monday.

Under the hood, you're getting a very premium experience for less than $45. The silky TMR joysticks have the durability of Hall Effect sticks, and GameSir uses micro switches for the face buttons and D-pad, giving you a tactile feedback with each input.

In addition, there are two buttons on the back that you can set up for custom macros or commands, and it lets you hook it up to your devices using either the 2.4 GHz adapter or Bluetooth. This is a no-nonsense gamepad for your PC or laptop and, thanks to that sale price, one that makes it a more affordable option for gamers. — Ben Stockton

The GameSir Cyclone 2 is a top quality controller for gamers. It's got a layout that's true to the standard Xbox gamepad, so it won't be a difficult one to adjust to. More importantly, though, is the price: it's down to $44.79, back at its record lowest on Amazon.

A hugely powerful RTX 5090 OLED gaming laptop from Lenovo is on sale at B&H Photo. You can score a Lenovo Legion Pro 7i for $3,999.99, down from $5,299.99, for as long as the stock holds out.

The model we're looking at here includes a 24-core Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU and a 175W RTX 5090 laptop GPU with 24GB of VRAM. That's not as beefy as the RTX 5090 on a desktop PC but, this is a laptop, so it can't quite reach those kinds of power demands.

Lenovo's Legion Pro 7i boasts a 24-core Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU and 175W RTX 5090 GPU with 24GB of VRAM. This is a high spec laptop for gaming that'll handle anything you can throw at it.

Otherwise, this top-end system comes with 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. More importantly, though, is that 16-inch OLED display, offering up 1600p gameplay at 240 Hz, with Nvidia G-Sync support to stop any screen tearing. You've got a high spec rig here with peformance on the top end of what you're able to achieve on laptop, and the $1,300 discount makes it all that sweeter.

You'll need to be quick, though. Stock is low on this one, so don't expect it to hold out forever. — Ben Stockton

Ever needed to duplicate a hard drive for a friend, family member, or for yourself as a quick backup? I've done this before to copy my main Windows installation drive over to a bigger one, for instance. Doing it manually is hard, but with this Rosewill M.2 cloner, you don't have to worry. This is one of those back-of-the-cupboard tools that you'll want in your arsenal, because you'll hate yourself when you don't. It's also down to a record low price of $32.29 right now.

This M.2 SSD cloner works with NVMe and AHCI drives (Key M), and lets you easily duplicate boot or storage drives with the press of a button. Note that it does not work with older SATA-based M.2 (Key B) drives.

Tom's Hardware staffers have used this drive duplicator before. You just need to plug it in, pop in your old M.2 drive into the left slot, place the new drive in the right slot, press the button, and wait for the magic to happen. You can also plug the whole thing into a PC and use software to duplicate your drive, which you might want to do if you're resizing partitions and going from a smaller to larger drive.

The $32.29 sale price makes this Rosewill M.2 cloner an easy buy. You won't always need it, but when you do, you won't be without out. It can take a tough storage situation and turn it into a 15-minute quick fix. — Ben Stockton

When I travel, I like to carry around a relatively beefy portable power bank with me to keep my devices charged. Whether I'm on an airplane, on a ferry, or sitting on the beach listening to some tunes, it's nice to be able to keep everything juiced up. To that end, UGREEN's Nexode 20000 mAh power bank is more than up to the task of serving as a mainstay in your travel bag. It usually retails for $89.99, but is on sale right now for $54.99.

The UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank supports up to 130W of combined power output and features two USB-C and one USB-A port.

The power bank supports up to 100W of total power output between its two USB-C ports. USB-C1 supports up to 100W output, while USB-C2 outputs up to 30W. Besides its two USB-C ports, there's also a single USB-A port.

According to UGREEN, the power bank can recharge a 13-inch MacBook Air up to 1.3 times, or it can recharge an iPhone 16 Pro up to 3.7 times. In addition, there's also a nifty smart LCD status indicator that tells you the current charge level of the battery, power output levels, and time remaining until the battery is discharged (or filled up, if it's recharging). — Brandon Hill

Hard drives are much more expensive than they used to be, so finding a deal is pretty tricky. This WD 20Tb Elements Desktop External Hard Drive is now $549, a 38% saving on the $879.99 list price. Notably, it's actually $230 cheaper than the 18TB version, and it's even cheaper than the 16TB model.

In theory, you could pop the drive out of this and use it as an internal hard drive, but there are no guarantees, and this can void your warranty, as is always the case.

The Western Digital Elements Desktop drive comes with 20TB of storage, connecting to your PC via USB with a USB 3.2 Gen 1 connection. It includes a 3.5-inch Western Digital HDD inside.

Western Digital doesn't specify the drive speed, but it's likely a 5,400 RPM drive inside, which is slow enough that the USB 3.0 connection won't hold back your transfer rates. You get a two-year limited warranty, though opening the enclosure to remove the drive will void your warranty. — Stephen Warwick

Hoto make some of our favorite PC building tools, and this 24-in-1 Multi Bit Mini Screwdriver Set is a lovely impulse buy at just $14. This is a great stocking filler for a holiday gift, or a personal pickup for anyone who does a bit of PC tinkering and tech DIY.

This Hoto 24-in-1 precision screwdriver with 24 different bits is the perfect addition to a hobbyist or 3D printer's toolkit.

This is a sleek, compact driver that has 24 double-ended bits crammed inside. The bits are rated at 60 HRC, and you get Torx, Phillips, Hex, and other shapes included. Grab it at this $13.99 sale price while you can. — Joe Shields

This unmanaged Ethernet switch is a massive upgrade for your home networking, and now a massive 54% off in Amazon's Black Friday sale. Split your bandwidth across seven different lines, and the switch will take care of routing your internet for you. Supports speeds of up to 2.5-Gigabit, with up to 40 Gbps of switching capacity.

The TL-SG108S-M2 offers 40 Gbps of switching capacity and supports devices at 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, or 2.5 Gbps speeds.

An 8-port switch for $60 is a standout deal that immediately grabbed my attention. To put it in perspective, I paid $59.97 for a 6-port UGREEN 2.5 GbE switch around this time last year.

With a total switching capacity of 40 Gbps, the TL-SG108S-M2 supports 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, and 2.5 Gbps connections. It easily handles everyday networking tasks—whether you are hooking up a desktop PC, connecting a NAS, setting up a shared workgroup printer, or running an access point to expand wireless coverage. Best of all, it works seamlessly over standard Cat5e wiring. — Brandon Hill

Get a massive saving on both versions of Logitech's G-series racing wheel and pedals, either the G29 for PS5 and PS4 version, or the G920 for Xbox Series X, S, and Xbox One. Both work with PC. The only difference is the console compatibility, and of course the corresponding button symbols.

The Logitech G29 racing wheel and pedals works with PC and Mac, and there are specific versions for PlayStation and Xbox consoles.

The G29 has been the go-to entry-level racing wheel for over a decade, and for good reason. You can spend well over $1,000 on a direct drive wheel, and that’s just for the wheel alone. For $199, Logitech offers real force feedback, a comfortable and ergonomic wheel, and a set of three pedals to get you started in any racing sim.

This isn't an all-time low for the G29, but it's close. We've seen it once, over five years ago, drop to $170. — Jake Roach

HyperX is known for its excellent line of gaming microphones — they're easy to use, they make you sound great, and they have a handy tap-to-mute button that works perfectly. While the QuadCast 2 S is the company's flagship mic with four polar patterns, most people only need one. And that's where the SoloCast 2 comes in.

This USB condenser microphone features just one polar pattern (cardioid), and is designed to pick up the voice of one person directly in front of it. It's a very sturdily built mic — a solid black cylinder with a metal grille, and it weighs almost 13 ounces (365.7g). But unlike most microphones, this actually hides a built-in stand. You can tilt the microphone back about 40 degrees (which angles it right at your face, if it's sitting on a desk). The bottom is lined with rubber so it won't slip around, and there's also a mounting point for those who would still prefer to mount it on a boom arm.

This 14mm electret condenser capsule mic features an integrated desktop stand that tilts the mic upward 40 degrees (there's a mounting point on the bottom of the stand, in case you do want to mount it on a boom arm). It has a cardioid polar pattern and sounds pretty good out of the box, and it features HyperX's signature tap-to-mute button on the top.

The mic has a USB-C port at the back and a large tap-to-mute button on top, as well as a red indicator light that lets you know when the mic is muted. The microphone records at a high-res 24-bit / 96 kHz bit-depth/sample rate, and it sounds very good out of the box. It has a built-in internal shock mount and pop filter, but it definitely benefits from being mounted instead of just sitting on your desk. However, it's nice to know the option is always there, thanks to the built-in desk stand.

It's a pretty simple mic, and it's already pretty budget-friendly at retail price. But now it's even cheaper — just $44.99 at HyperX, down $15 from its original price of $59.99. You can read my full review here. — Sarah

This nifty and compact Razer Huntsman Mini 60% Wired keyboard has fallen to a new lowest-ever price of $65.54, exactly have price! Specifically, this is the linear optical switches version in black, although you can also pick up the white version for just $69.

The Razer Huntsman Mini 60% Wired is a mechanical keyboard with Razer's optical linear switches, offering adjustable actuation points and Razer's Snap Tap feature.

With Razer's optical switches, you can use Razer's Snap Tap feature to rapidly swap between two key presses, as well as rebind commands to different actuation points on the key press. The keyboard is primarily constructed out of plastic, though Razer uses an aluminum top frame for a bit of premium flair. — Stephen Warwick

Creality's K2 Combo was just $399 in the October sales, and now it has fallen to the even more enticing price of $349, $200 off! With a 260 x 260 x 260mm print area, it's a great small option.

Creality's K2 Combo is a formidable 3D printer. The smallest of the K2 family of printers, the K2 Combo still has a 260 x 260 x 260 mm print size, allowing users to print large objects inside its enclosed frame without worrying about having to glue together multiple prints. #10373. Holotron-12B - High Throughput Computer Use Agent

We're thrilled to release Holotron-12B, a multimodal computer-use model from H Company. Post-trained from the open NVIDIA Nemotron-Nano-2 VL model on H Company’s proprietary data mixture, Holotron-12B is the result of a close collaboration between our research labs to engineer a new type of model optimized primarily for scale and performance in production.

H Company is part of the NVIDIA Inception Program.

The model is now available on Hugging Face.

Most multimodal models today optimize primarily for static vision or following instructions. Holotron-12B, just like our Holo2 model, however, has a different goal: serving as a policy model for computer-use agents that must perceive, decide, and act efficiently in interactive environments.

With Holotron-12B, we wanted to create a model that could efficiently and effectively scale in production while handling long contexts with multiple images, and still perform well on agent benchmarks. The NVIDIA Nemotron model offered a strong foundation on the inference side, and by developing Holotron-12B we've demonstrated how much more the model can accomplish with further training.

Holotron-12B's significant leap in inference efficiency is made possible by its foundational Nemotron architecture, which utilizes a hybrid State-Space Model (SSM) and attention mechanism. Unlike purely transformer-based models, this design is optimized for high-throughput serving. State-space models offer superior scalability for long-context inference by avoiding the quadratic computation cost associated with the full attention mechanism, particularly benefiting agentic workloads involving multiple images and lengthy interaction histories. In terms of inference, the main contribution of an SSM is its dramatically reduced memory-footprint: while vanilla attention stores K and V activations per token and layer (the notorious KV Cache), SSMs are a linear recurrent model, storing only a constant state per layer per generated sequence, independent of the length of the sequence.

When evaluated on the WebVoyager Benchmark, the model excels using a real-world multimodal agentic workload featuring long context, multiple high-resolution images, and a high request concurrency of 100 benchmark workers. Running on a single H100 GPU and using vLLM with the latest SSM optimizations (v0.14.1), Holotron-12B achieved an over 2x higher throughput compared to Holo2-8B. This makes Holotron-12B an attractive choice for throughput-bound workloads, such as data generation, annotation, and online reinforcement learning.

In a controlled experiment setup (see figure 2), Holotron-12B continues to scale efficiently as concurrency increases, with total token throughput rising steadily to 8.9k tokens/s at a max concurrency of 100. In contrast, the total token throughput of Holo2-8B plateaus much more quickly at 5.1k tokens/s. This behaviour highlights a key strength of the Nemotron architecture, namely more effective and efficient VRAM utilization, and smaller overall memory footprint, which allows much larger effective batch sizes on the same hardware. Even at large batch sizes, Holotron-12B maintains strong throughput.

Holotron-12B was trained in two stages. We started from Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2-VL-BF16, a multimodal base model published by NVIDIA. We then performed supervised fine-tuning on H Company’s proprietary localization and navigation data mixture, focusing on screen understanding, grounding, and UI-level interactions.

The final checkpoint was trained on approximately 14 billion tokens.

On computer-use and navigation benchmarks, Holotron-12B shows strong improvements over the Nemotron base model and strong performance with established agent models. Its WebVoyager performance increased from 35.1% to 80.5%, exceeding Holo2-8B’s performance on the benchmark and illustrating the model’s ability to perform effectively in an agentic setting.

Holotron-12B also improves substantially over the base Nemotron model on localization and grounding benchmarks such as OS-World-G, GroundUI, and WebClick.

Holotron-12B demonstrates that the NVIDIA Nemotron VL model provides a strong foundation for real-world multimodal agents when paired with the right training setup and infrastructure work.

The model offers strong agent performance, significantly improved inference throughput, and a clear path for future improvements, particularly around higher-resolution vision training.

We look forward to seeing what others build with Holotron-12B. The model and checkpoints are available now on Hugging Face under an NVIDIA Open Model License.

NVIDIA announced today the release of Nemotron 3 Omni. Building on the success of Holotron-12B, we are preparing to post-train this next generation of multimodal models. By leveraging the enhanced hybrid SSM-Attention and MoE architectural foundations of the Nemotron 3 family, we aim to deliver even greater leaps in reasoning capabilities and multimodal precision with the newly announced Nemotron 3 Omni. As this evolution pushes Holotron beyond research and into a commercial application, it will provide enterprises with the high-throughput, low-latency performance required for massive-scale autonomous "computer use" deployments.

#10372. New OpenAI and Anthropic models sound alarms on safety and control, report

Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies.

While both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that new models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting new safety practices while Anthropic said that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”

#10370. Samsung officially starts rolling out Wear OS 7 to these older Galaxy Watch models

Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update.

Samsung’s One UI 9 Watch update is largely focused on new health features including Vitals, Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and improvements to both Sleep Coaching and Sleep Apnea alerts.

“Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range.

One UI 9 Watch is based on Wear OS 7, and also includes an improved Compass app with “Track Back,” a feature that helps users to follow their route back to a recorded point.

There’s also a new “Portrait Watch Face” that can adjust the clock face around the subject of a photo.

Samsung is, as of today, officially rolling out One UI 9 Watch with Wear OS 7 to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. Meanwhile, the update is in beta for several other older models which will be updated soon including:

The Galaxy Watch 5 series and Watch FE should also be getting the update, but no beta is available for those devices. Samsung’s first Wear OS watches, the Galaxy Watch 4 series, will not get the update.

#10369. How to Build a Unified Lead Tracking Pipeline for Web Forms and Phone Calls

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report shows two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:

const params = new URL(url).searchParams;

"utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign",

return Object.fromEntries(keys.flatMap(key => {

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",

The event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

"form.submitted", "call.started", "call.completed",

export function makeEvent(input, trusted) {

const ids = [trusted.tenantId, trusted.source,

if (ids.some(id => typeof id !== "string" ||

throw new TypeError("Invalid event identifiers");

throw new TypeError("Unsupported event type");

const time = Date.parse(input.occurredAt);

if (typeof input.occurredAt !== "string" ||

new Date(time).toISOString() !== input.occurredAt) {

throw new TypeError("Expected a canonical UTC timestamp");

attribution_ref: input.attributionRef ?? null,

Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

For a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a new one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id)

The ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.

export async function persistEvent(pool, event) {

const key = [event.tenant_id, event.source, event.event_id];

const values = [...key, JSON.stringify(event)];

await client.query("BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED");

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, source, event_id) DO NOTHING

WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND source = $2 AND event_id = $3

const error = new Error("Event ID reused with new data");

INSERT INTO crm_outbox (tenant_id, source, event_id)

return { inserted: inserted.rowCount === 1 };

PostgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a new event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

#10368. State of Open Source on Hugging Face: Spring 2026

This post examines how the open source AI landscape has shifted across competition, geography, technical trends, and emerging communities over the past year. We primarily examine community activity on Hugging Face across many types of metrics to give a holistic view of the ecosystem.

This post builds on an earlier analysis conducted mid-2025, available here, which examined what the Hugging Face Community is building. We recommend reading additional perspectives on the open source ecosystem in and outside of Hugging Face from the Data Provenance Initiative, Interconnects, OpenRouter and a16z, and MIT and the Linux Foundation. As the Hugging Face ecosystem is distributed, analyses are a combination of Hugging Face and community members' work, each of which is appropriately credited.

Activity in the open source AI ecosystem has rapidly grown, with the number of users, model, and dataset repositories all close to doubling. In 2025, Hugging Face grew to 13 million users, more than 2 million public models, and over 500,000 public datasets. This growth signals more than increased interest in open source; it reflects a shift toward active participation, with users increasingly creating derivative artifacts such as fine-tuned models, adapters, benchmarks, and applications rather than only consuming pre-trained systems.

Data from Hugging Face | Hugging Face's two million models and counting: Graph and story by AI World

The ecosystem remains highly concentrated. Approximately half of the models on Hugging Face have less than 200 total downloads, and the top 200 most downloaded models, or 0.01% of models, comprise 49.6% of all downloads.

Specialized communities form around particular domains, languages, or problem areas, and often show sustained engagement and reuse even when their overall download counts are modest. Open source AI is best understood as a collection of overlapping sub-ecosystems rather than a single uniform market.

More companies, both large and small, are building on open source. Over 30% of the Fortune 500 now maintain verified accounts on Hugging Face. Startups frequently use open models as default components: Thinking Machines built its Tinker model options entirely on open weights, while popular IDEs such as VSCode and Cursor support both open and closed models. Established American companies such as Airbnb have increased their engagement with the open ecosystem, and Hugging Face has seen more legacy companies upgrading their organizational subscriptions over the course of 2025.

Big Tech companies are frequently creating new repositories on Hugging Face Hub; visualized side-by-side, the strong increase in repository growth shows investment over time. NVIDIA has emerged as the strongest contributor.

Data from Hugging Face | Big Tech Is All-In On Open-Source AI, Graph and story by AI World

Studies of open software more broadly suggest that the downstream value created by open artifacts far exceeds the cost of producing them. Similar dynamics are emerging in AI, where open models are reused, adapted, and specialized across thousands of downstream applications. Organizations that rely exclusively on closed systems often incur higher costs and face reduced flexibility in deployment and customization.

All-time downloads over the past four years show clear frontrunner regions in model popularity. The U.S. and China have historically been top contributors, with the UK, Germany, and France as secondary in popularity. Models developed by individual users or distributed organizations without a clear geographic base account for about half of all platform downloads.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”

The geographic composition of the open source ecosystem has fundamentally changed. Hugging Face data shows China surpassing the U.S. in monthly downloads and overall downloads. In the past year, Chinese models quickly accounted for the plurality or 41% of downloads.

Industry's share of overall development fell from around 70% before 2022 to roughly 37% in 2025. Meanwhile, independent or unaffiliated developers rose from 17% to 39% of all downloads over the same period, at times accounting for more than half of total usage. Individuals and small collectives focused on quantizing, adapting, and redistributing base models. These intermediaries now steer a meaningful portion of what typical users can run and how innovations spread through the ecosystem.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”

Different regions contribute in different ways. The United States and Western Europe have historically dominated through large industry labs (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Stability AI), while China has increasingly led on both releases and adoption. France, Germany, and the UK continue to contribute through research organizations, national AI initiatives, and specialized model families. Ecosystems supporting a variety of contributors and organizational forms tend to produce more widely adopted artifacts.

Popular models from startups were more widespread. Competitive countries were France and South Korea. Notably, the fourth most popular entity for developing new trending models were individual users, not organizations. Creating competitive models at a user level is more accessible than ever before.

Of the newly created models in 2025, the majority of trending models were either developed in China or derivative of a model developed in China. The most popular models were developed by large organizations, predominantly from the U.S. and China. For more on the Chinese AI ecosystem, read our three part series reflecting on the changes in one year since the "DeepSeek Moment", with one on strategic changes, two on architectural changes, and three on organizations and the future.

In 2025, China’s AI ecosystem steered heavily into open source, following the viral release of DeepSeek’s R1 model in January. The number of competitive Chinese organizations releasing models and the number of repositories on Hugging Face skyrocketed. Baidu went from zero releases on the Hub in 2024 to over 100 in 2025. ByteDance and Tencent each increased releases by eight to nine times. Organizations that had previously favored closed approaches, including Baidu and MiniMax, shifted decisively toward open releases.

A similar number of popular U.S. organizations have consistently contributed a higher volume of repositories over time. Meta and its former Facebook research organization account for a significant proportion of open releases, as does Google to a lesser extent.

Next to each other, the steep upward trajectory of repository growth among popular Chinese organizations emerges as a key strategic difference.

Open source AI is increasingly tied to questions of sovereignty. Open weight models allow governments and public institutions to fine-tune systems on local data under national legal frameworks. Models that can be deployed on domestic hardware reduce reliance on foreign-controlled cloud infrastructure. Transparency around model architecture, training processes, and evaluation supports regulatory review and public accountability. Read more about the open source approach to sovereignty here.

At the national level, governments are taking action. South Korea's National Sovereign AI Initiative launched mid-2025 named national champions LG AI Research, SK Telecom, Naver Cloud, NC AI, and Upstage to produce competitive domestic models. Three models from South Korea trended simultaneously on Hugging Face Hub in February 2026. In March 2026, In 2026, South Korea and U.S. startup Reflection AI announced a data center partnership, also bringing frontier open weight models to South Korea.

Switzerland's Swiss AI initiative and various EU-funded projects reflect similar priorities. The UK's principle of "public money, public code" has influenced several government-backed AI initiatives.

These investments in open-source and open weight AI are already paying dividends for countries with thriving AI training ecosystems of their own, as we see that models and datasets are typically most used in the regions where they're developed; with developers often turning to the models that best represent their languages and reflect similar technical and application requirements.

Most liked models on the Hub show community attention, in terms of ability to go back to or reference the model or general popularity. While this metric does not always reflect usage, the attention collected over time can show signals of interest. In one year, the most liked models went from predominantly U.S.-developed from Meta’s Llama family, to an international mix with China’s DeepSeek-R1 at the top.

While determining the value of scientific contributions can be determined by many metrics, our upvote feature on the Hub shows papers from large AI organizations be widely appreciated by community members. Notably, the most upvoted papers are from large organizations, mostly from the U.S. and China. The majority of the top organizations are Chinese Big Tech companies, with ByteDance sharing a high volume of high impact papers.

Space by Hugging Face | PaperVerse Explorer

Of Hugging Face's Daily Papers, a set of papers curated by Hugging Face's AK, papers that reference model and dataset creation, showing the most open source adoption, are generally diverse. Prominent takeaways show medical papers being influential, while Big Tech's influence is sparse.

Data from Hugging Face | Graphic and story by AI World

How our community members choose to build on models, whether via fine-tuning, merging, or other methods, reflects model popularity and usability. Alibaba as an organization has more derivative models than both Google and Meta combined, with the Qwen family constituting more than 113,000 derivative models. When including all models that tag Qwen, that number balloons to over 200,000 models.

Model development has increasingly emphasized accessibility alongside scale. Smaller models are downloaded and deployed at far higher rates than very large systems, reflecting practical constraints around cost, latency, and hardware availability.

This small-model dominance occurs in part because far more models are released at that size. But even when normalizing for this, the data from the ATOM Project's Relative Adoption Metric shows that the median top-10 models from 1-9B parameters are only downloaded about 4x more than models above 100B. Automated systems and CI pipelines further inflate small model download counts, but the trend toward smaller, deployable models is real.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Article by ATOM

Engagement with open models tends to peak almost immediately after release, then slow. Mean engagement duration is approximately 6 weeks. Continuous improvement and frequent updates have become critical for maintaining relevance. DeepSeek's successive releases (V3, R1, V3.2) kept it competitive even as challengers emerged. Organizations that stagnate in development tend to lose share quickly to those with frequent updates or domain-specific fine-tunes.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Choksi et al. "The Brief and Wondrous Life of Open Models"

The mean size of downloaded open models rose from 827M parameters in 2023 to 20.8B in 2025, driven largely by quantization and mixture-of-experts architectures. The median, however, increased only marginally, from 326M to 406M parameters. This divergence indicates that high-end LLM users are pulling up the mean while underlying small-model usage remains stable.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. "Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem"

Performance differences between frontier models and smaller systems often narrow rapidly through fine-tuning and task-specific adaptation. On the Hub, models with hundreds of millions of parameters support search, tagging, and document processing workflows, while models in the single-digit billions are widely used for coding, reasoning, and multimodal tasks. As a result, most major model developers now release families of models spanning a range of sizes. The rise of capable small models shifts autonomy closer to the edge, reducing dependency on centralized cloud providers.

Open source AI development is closely linked to hardware trends. Most models are optimized for NVIDIA GPUs, but support for AMD hardware continues to expand. Stability AI model collections now optimize for both NVIDIA and AMD platforms. Libraries increasingly target both, and tooling has improved to make cross-hardware deployment more straightforward. In 2025 Hugging Face launched the Kernel Hub to load and run kernels optimized for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

In parallel, Chinese open models are being released with explicit support for domestically developed chips. Alibaba has invested in inference-focused chip architectures designed to fill Chinese data centers with hardware capable of running open source models locally.

While access to compute remains a core necessity across the board for development and deployment of AI models, open-source and open-weight models are helping break away from an ecosystem where it becomes the be-all and end-all, with increasingly more models at all levels of performance pushing efficiency from 10x to 1000x lower costs than flagship AI models the largest developers.

Still, the question of infrastructure investment for open source remains urgent. Public funding for data centers capable of training and serving open models has become a growing policy discussion, particularly in Europe and the UK. The gap between the compute resources available to large closed-model companies and those accessible to the open source community continues to shape what is feasible in open development.

Robotics has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sub-communities on Hugging Face. The numbers are striking: robotics datasets grew from 1,145 in 2024 to 26,991 in 2025, climbing from rank 44 to the single largest dataset category on the Hub in just three years. For comparison, text generation, the second-largest category, had only around 5,000 datasets in 2025.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Story by AI World

Community-contributed datasets span everything from household manipulation tasks to autonomous driving. The largest multimodal dataset for spatial intelligence, Learning to Drive (L2D), was released through a LeRobot collaboration with Yaak. Datasets like RoboMIND, with over 107,000 real-world trajectories across 479 distinct tasks and multiple robot embodiments, provide the kind of scale and diversity needed for training generalizable robotic policies.

Hugging Face's acquisition of Pollen Robotics opened open source robotic sales to both industry and academic labs, as well as everyday hobbyists. LeRobot, Hugging Face's open source robotics library that provides models, datasets, and tools for real-world robotics in PyTorch, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and vision-language-action models, experienced rapid growth. Over the past year, its GitHub repository stars nearly tripled.

Data from GitHub | Graphic from star-history.com

Scientific research has become another particularly active area. Open models and datasets are increasingly used for protein folding, molecular dynamics, drug discovery, and scientific data analysis. All frontier AI companies now have dedicated science teams, though much current focus remains on literature discovery rather than direct experimentation.

Space by Hugging Face | Science Release Heatmap

Community-led projects have formed around shared research goals, often involving hundreds of contributors working across institutions and disciplines. These efforts highlight the role of open source as a mechanism for coordinating large-scale, interdisciplinary work that would be difficult to organize through traditional academic or corporate structures alone.

The open source AI ecosystem continues to evolve through a combination of global participation, technical specialization, and institutional adoption. Several trends are likely to define the next phase.

The geographic rebalancing of power is accelerating. Western organizations increasingly seek commercially deployable alternatives to Chinese models, creating urgency around efforts like OpenAI's GPT-OSS, AI2's OLMo, and Google's Gemma to offer competitive open options from US and European developers. Whether these efforts can match the adoption momentum of Qwen and DeepSeek will be a defining question of 2026.

The growth of sub-communities in robotics and science suggests that open source AI is expanding beyond language and image generation into the physical and experimental domains. The infrastructure, norms, and coordination mechanisms developed around text and image models are being adapted for new modalities and use cases.

For researchers, developers, companies, and governments, open source remains a foundational layer for building, evaluating, and governing AI systems. With increasing agent deployments, open-source and its interoperability will be key for agents to thrive. Its trajectory over the past year makes one thing clear: the open source ecosystem is where much of the practical work of AI development, adaptation, and deployment takes place, and its influence on the broader AI landscape continues to grow.

Thank you to the Hugging Face community for continuing to build the foundation of the AI ecosystem 🤗
